title: How much is left when four sevenths go from six sevenths?
description: A strip is cut into seven equal parts and six of them are shaded. Four shaded parts are taken away, and the parts that stay show what is left. Keeko's doubt is that the bottom numbers are taken away as well.
teaching_notes: One idea: when two fractions count the same fractional unit, take away the top numbers and keep the bottom number. Watch for students who take away the bottom numbers too.

video_script.why: The child sees that taking away fractions of the same fractional unit is taking away shaded parts of one strip, so only the count of parts changes.
video_script.substitution: The book's rectangular strip cut into seven equal parts; each part is one seventh.
video_script.anchor: a rectangular strip cut into seven equal parts with six parts shaded, as in the book
video_script.wrong_answer: take away the tops and take away the bottoms
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko takes away the tops and the bottoms, so the bottom becomes zero; a strip cannot be cut into zero parts, and every part left is still one seventh, so the idea is broken.
video_script.payoff_line: Six sevenths take away four sevenths leaves two sevenths
video_script.fraction_reading: one seventh, four sevenths, six sevenths, two sevenths
never_show: the remaining fraction before the answer beat
maths_rules: the strip is cut into 7 equal parts, so each part is 1/7 of the strip
4/7 is 4 parts of 1/7, taken away from the 6 shaded parts
6 − 4 = 2, so 2 shaded parts of 1/7 are left
Keeko's slip: 7 − 7 = 0, and a strip cannot be cut into 0 parts
video_script.design: One strip, one idea: same fractional unit, so take away the number of parts and keep the unit. The strip stays on the board from start to end.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a rectangular strip cut into 7 equal parts with 6 parts shaded; the words 6/7 − 4/7 appear above the strip

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.strip: the strip of 7 equal parts appears with 6 parts shaded
marks.ask: the words 6/7 − 4/7 appear and 4 shaded parts glow

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about taking away fractions.
<bookmark mark='strip'/>A strip is cut into seven equal parts, and six of the parts are shaded.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>We want to take away four sevenths from the six sevenths. How much of the strip is left?

beats.on_screen: the strip holds still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the strip with each of its 7 parts labelled 1/7; under 6/7 and under 4/7 the label same unit 1/7 appears

marks.unit: each part of the strip is labelled 1/7
marks.same: the label same unit 1/7 appears under both fractions

narration: <bookmark mark='unit'/>Each part of the strip is one seventh. This size of part is called the fractional unit.
<bookmark mark='count'/>Six sevenths means six of these parts. Four sevenths means four of these parts.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Both fractions count the same fractional unit, one seventh.

beats.on_screen: Given: 6/7 of the strip is shaded; take away 4/7; both are parts of 1/7

marks.given: the two fractions are written on the working board

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, six sevenths of the strip are shaded, and we take away four sevenths.

beats.on_screen: To find: how much of the strip is left, 6/7 − 4/7

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how much of the strip is left.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: unit of 6/7 is 1/7; unit of 4/7 is 1/7; the units match

marks.same: the two units 1/7 are written side by side with a tick between them

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Step one, check the fractional unit, because we can only take away parts of the same size.
Both fractions are counted in sevenths, so the unit matches.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: take away 4 shaded parts: 6 − 4; 4 shaded parts slide off the strip

marks.take: 4 shaded parts slide off the strip

narration: <bookmark mark='take'/>Step two, take away four of the shaded parts, because we take away four sevenths.
<bookmark mark='count'/>The number of parts is six take away four.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 6 − 4 = 2 parts of 1/7 stay; the bottom number 7 stays

marks.left: the 2 shaded parts that stay light up one by one
marks.bottom: the bottom number 7 stays the same

narration: <bookmark mark='left'/>Step three, count the shaded parts that stay. Six take away four leaves two parts.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>Each part is still one seventh, so the bottom number stays seven.

marks.ans: the answer 2/7 is boxed and the 2 shaded parts glow

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Six sevenths take away four sevenths leaves two sevenths of the strip.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the strip
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: tops 6 − 4 = 2 and bottoms 7 − 7 = 0, giving 2 over 0; an empty outline with no parts; the bubble is struck through; the strip with 7 parts returns

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows tops and bottoms both taken away
marks.zero: an empty outline with no parts appears and the 0 glows
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and the strip of 7 parts returns

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we take away the tops and take away the bottoms.
Six take away four leaves two, but seven take away seven leaves zero.
<bookmark mark='zero'/>That would make two over zero, a strip cut into no parts at all.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Nobody cut the strip again. It still has seven parts, and each part is still one seventh.
Only the number of parts changed, so the bottom number stays.
